newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian wheat growers to own AWB - minister.
newsitem.headline: Australian wheat growers to own AWB - minister.

text.p: Australian Primary Industries Minister John Anderson announced on Thursday the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) would become a private grower-owned company under a major corporate restructuring of the statutory body.
But the privatised AWB's export monopoly of Australian wheat would be retained under law, he said.
As part of the restructuring, two classes of shares would be issued -- A-class shares to wheat growers and B-class shares to equity holders in the grower-financed Wheat Industry Fund (WIF).
The new grower-owned company would be responsible for all aspects of wheat marketing, Anderson said in a statement.
"This will place ownership and control of marketing in the hands of the growers so the industry can control its own future," Anderson said.
Anderson had previously said the move was the first step towards the likely listing of the AWB on the Australian stock exchange after the year 2000.
He said A-class shares would be issued at nominal value, be non-transferable and redeemed as holders left the industry or failed to qualify as wheat growers. Dividends would not be paid.
A-class shareholders would have the right to vote for the majority of directors, while B-class holders would be able to elect a minority of directors.
B-class shares would be issued to WIF equity holders in proportion to their equity in the fund. B-class shareholders would receive a commercial rate of return.
The WIF would also be converted into shares to provide the capital backing to allow the company to operate in its own right when the government guarantee of AWB borrowings ended in 1999.
The restructure also provided for the removal of the two percent levy on wheat sales for WIF purposes on June 30, 1999.

Anderson said the restructure was based on a Grains Council of Australia-developed model, which provided for the retention of the single export desk, commercial flexibility and industry self-determination.
"I believe the model successfully balances the objectives of grower ownership and control, and commerciality," Anderson said.
"The single desk will be enshrined in legislation to provide the industry with the surety it requires," he said.
"The new commercial structure will ensure the very best use is made of the export monopoly and assist its retention in the longer term."

Anderson said he believed the restructure optimised the AWB's chances of a favourable outcome in the 1999 government competition policy review, when the AWB's monopoly on wheat export sales would be considered.
The first step of the restructure would occur from October 1 when a subsidiary of the AWB was created to undertake its commercial activities, he said.
